Chapter 2: Finding a Voice in a World of Double Standards
Stepping into adulthood, she carried with her the lessons from childhood—resilience, a sharp sense of humor, and a knack for observing the world around her. But the world she entered? Well, it wasn’t always friendly to women who spoke up or refused to fit into tidy little boxes.
Those early jobs? They were a mix of the boring and the downright bizarre—waiting tables, helping customers in retail, and figuring out all those unspoken rules. You know the ones: where women are expected to smile, nod, and keep their opinions to themselves.
But comedy? Now, that was a different story. On stage, she could say things most people only dared to think. Honesty was her currency, and laughter was the payoff. Still, even in comedy, the rules changed if you were a woman. Audiences—and sometimes the folks running the show—expected her to walk a fine line. Be funny, but not too edgy. Be confident, but not intimidating. Attractive, but in a way that wouldn’t make anyone uncomfortable.
The pressure to blend in was always there. Step out of line, and the pushback came fast.
In those early days, she stood in front of rooms packed with strangers—people who doubted whether a woman could really be funny. There were nights when her jokes just didn’t land, when hecklers tried to throw her off, or when club owners made it clear she was only there to fill a quota, not because they believed in her talent.
Each of those moments, though, became a lesson. She learned to stand tall, to wield humor as both armor and a weapon, and to turn awkward silences into moments of connection.
And it wasn’t just on stage. In meetings and auditions, she was often sized up on her looks instead of her material. Comments about her body, her clothes, even the sound of her voice—these were all just part of the deal. She realized pretty quickly that women in comedy had to work twice as hard just to get half the recognition.
But instead of shrinking away, she leaned into her own authenticity. She refused to apologize for who she was or what she found funny.
And sure, sometimes that honesty made people uncomfortable. Jokes about sex, relationships, or body image? Suddenly, those were “too much” coming from a woman, even though male comedians talked about the same stuff all the time. But she knew that being open about these things mattered—not just for her, but for anyone who’d ever felt judged or silenced.
By owning her truth, she helped others feel like they could own theirs too.
Over time, her willingness to be vulnerable turned into her biggest strength. Audiences started to see themselves in her stories—about awkward dates, family chaos, or moments of self-doubt. Turns out, most people crave honesty, even if it makes them squirm at first.
The more she shared, the more she realized that laughter could break down barriers and challenge old stereotypes.
Of course, the journey had its price. There were days when the criticism stung, when doubts crept in, and the urge to just fit in felt so tempting.
But every time, she came back to those childhood lessons—resilience, the power of humor, the importance of accepting herself.
In a world that so often tried to quiet women, she found her voice…and used it to carve out a space where others could find theirs too.
